fetched_contents.text: Impact of Oxidative Stress in Fetal Programming Abstract Intrauterine stress induces increased risk of adult disease through fetal programming mechanisms. Oxidative stress can be generated by several conditions, such as, prenatal hypoxia, maternal under- and overnutrition, and excessive glucocorticoid exposure. The role of oxidant molecules as signaling factors in fetal programming via epigenetic mechanisms is discussed. By linking oxidative stress with dysregulation of specific target genes, we may be able to develop therapeutic strategies that protect against organ dysfunction in the programmed offspring. 1. Introduction This paper addresses the emerging role of oxidant molecules in fetal programming. Oxidative stress is associated with the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which have both physiologic and pathologic roles in the placenta [1], embryo [2], and the fetus [3–5]. We will address recent reviews and current studies that present evidence identifying the impact of oxidative stress on the fetus and how it may contribute to the permanent alterations in the offspring through programming mechanisms. 2. Intrauterine Stress and Fetal Programming Epidemiological evidence and animal model studies have identified a clear association between low birth weight and an increased incidence of hypertension, type II diabetes, metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and obesity [6–9]. This was first reported by Dr. David Barker in relation to the inverse relationship between birth weight and mortality rate due to cardiovascular disease [10–12] and systolic blood pressure [13]. Subsequently, babies of higher than normal birth weight were shown to have increased risk of metabolic disorders as adults [14, 15]. Extensive study has lead to identifying additional factors that include altered nutrition, glucocorticoid exposure, and prenatal hypoxia as intrauterine stressors initiating fetal programming [8, 9]. The relationship between adult disease (e.g., hypertension, insulin resistance, diabetes) and birth weight forms a U-shape curve demonstrating increased risk with both low [10–12] and high birth weight [16, 17]. The impact of intrauterine stress on the affected offspring is influenced by the severity and duration of the insult, as well as, the gestational age of fetal exposure [8, 9]. In conditions of maternal undernutrition, the fetus adapts by reducing its metabolic energy supply to protect critical organs for survival, first described as the Thrifty Phenotype Hypothesis [18]. With further study, the Predictive Adaptive Hypothesis was proposed to describe the fetal response to an anticipated undernourished postnatal environment [19]. Overnutrition (i.e., high fat and carbohydrate diet) during pregnancy also imposes an intrauterine challenge because the fetus is unable to properly regulate its nutrient excess, resulting in a greater than normal birth weight [20]. This is likely due to an imbalance of the appropriate complement of nutrients required for proper development of the fetal organs [9, 21]. Thus, high or low birth weight, resulting from altered growth patterns during intrauterine stress, carries an increased risk of adult disease for the offspring [6–9]. 3. Role of Oxidative Stress in Normal Fetal Development The development of the embryo occurs in a relatively low-oxygen environment. It is highly sensitive to injury to oxidant molecules because of its low antioxidant capacity [22, 23]. As placentation progresses, there is increased oxygen transfer, which increases the cellular generation of ROS [1]. This initiates a switch in the cellular redox state, from reduced to oxidized, acting as a driving force for cell differentiation [23, 24]. ROS serve as signaling molecules that induce transcription of several genes (e.g. HIF1A, CREB1, NFKB1) important in oxygen sensing, cell differentiation, and proliferation [1, 24, 25]. With placental maturation, there is increased oxygen transfer to the developing fetus, which is required for sustaining the increased metabolic rate during the rapid fetal growth phase [2].While both nutrition and oxygenation are important for fetal growth, identifying the specific effect of hypoxia in the absence of altered nutrition is important for understanding the role of hypoxia in fetal programming. Recent study has identified the effect of reduced oxygenation, independent of nutrition, using a chick embryo model [26]. Incubation of fertilized eggs from hens at high-altitude resulted in reduced fetal growth compared to eggs obtained from hens at sea level. The restricted fetal growth occurring at high-altitude was corrected by incubating fertilized eggs from high-altitude hens at sea level or by oxygen supplementation that matched sea level conditions. Thus, in the presence of adequate nutrition, reduced oxygenation can negatively impact normal growth and development. Recent animal studies have identified an important role of oxidant molecules in fetal cardiovascular function under normal conditions [3–5]. Antioxidant administration of melatonin or vitamin C to pregnant sheep increased umbilical vascular [5] and fetal femoral artery conductance [4], respectively, by mechanisms associated with increased nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability following decreased superoxide anion levels. In addition, inhibition of superoxide anion generation by allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, attenuated the fetal sheep pressor responses to phenylephrine and enhanced umbilical vascular conductance by altering NO bioavailability and activation of β1 adrenoceptor mechanisms, respectively [3]. Thus, oxidant molecules play an important physiological role in normal fetal cardiovascular homeostasis. A delicate balance may exist between optimal oxygen levels and the generation of ROS molecules during gestational periods of embryonic and fetal development. 4. fetched_contents.text: Maternal Undernutrition Significantly Impacts Ovarian Follicle Number and Increases Ovarian Oxidative Stress in Adult Rat Offspring Abstract Background We have shown recently that maternal undernutrition (UN) advanced female pubertal onset in a manner that is dependent upon the timing of UN. The long-term consequence of this accelerated puberty on ovarian function is unknown. Recent findings suggest that oxidative stress may be one mechanism whereby early life events impact on later physiological functioning. Therefore, using an established rodent model of maternal UN at critical windows of development, we examined maternal UN-induced changes in offspring ovarian function and determined whether these changes were underpinned by ovarian oxidative stress. Methodology/Principal Findings Our study is the first to show that maternal UN significantly reduced primordial and secondary follicle number in offspring in a manner that was dependent upon the timing of maternal UN. Specifically, a reduction in these early stage follicles was observed in offspring born to mothers undernourished throughout both pregnancy and lactation. Additionally, antral follicle number was reduced in offspring born to all mothers that were UN regardless of whether the period of UN was restricted to pregnancy or lactation or both. These reductions were associated with decreased mRNA levels of genes critical for follicle maturation and ovulation. Increased ovarian protein carbonyls were observed in offspring born to mothers UN during pregnancy and/or lactation and this was associated with peroxiredoxin 3 hyperoxidation and reduced mRNA levels; suggesting compromised antioxidant defence. This was not observed in offspring of mothers UN during lactation alone. Conclusions We propose that maternal UN, particularly at a time-point that includes pregnancy, results in reduced offspring ovarian follicle numbers and mRNA levels of regulatory genes and may be mediated by increased ovarian oxidative stress coupled with a decreased ability to repair the resultant oxidative damage. Together these data are suggestive of maternal UN potentially contributing to premature ovarian ageing in offspring. Introduction There is now considerable epidemiological and experimental evidence indicating that early life environmental signals, including nutrition, affect subsequent development leading to patho-physiologies including obesity and insulin resistance [1]. These signals induce highly integrated responses in endocrine-related homeostasis, resulting in persistent changes to the developmental trajectory producing an altered adult phenotype. This phenomenon has been termed developmental programming, whereby early life events trigger processes that prepare the individual for particular circumstances that are anticipated in the postnatal environment [1]–[3]. However, where the intrauterine and postnatal environments differ markedly, such modifications to the developmental trajectory may prove maladaptive in later life [3]. Evidence that reproductive maturation and function is similarly influenced by early life events is now emerging from animal studies and human populations [4], [5]. It is also clear that in many cases the prenatal and postnatal nutritional environments interact to influence reproductive function in offspring [4], [5]. Ovarian function is exquisitely sensitive to nutritional status and clinical and experimental studies have demonstrated that a decline in ovarian follicular reserve, changes in ovulation rates and altered age at onset of menarche are all vulnerable to early life influences [5], [6]. We have previously shown that nutritional deficits and excesses during intrauterine, lactational and post-weaning periods resulted in the acceleration of pubertal onset and subsequent changes in ovarian function [5]. The mechanisms underlying these changes however are unclear. Regulatory factors known to influence reproduction have become a focus of investigation and studies have demonstrated that, in addition to its role in energy metabolism, the adipokine leptin acts as a metabolic signal to the central reproductive axis [7]. Leptin has been reported to have both stimulatory and inhibitory actions on ovulatory processes and ovarian steroidogenesis [8], [9] and act as a permissive neuro-regulatory factor for the onset of puberty [10]–[12]. It has been suggested that altered oxidative stress conditions may underpin many of the known associations between early life nutritional adversity and altered later life physiologic function [13], [14]. In this regard, it has been shown that mitochondrial function was altered in embryos and oocytes of mothers that were nutritionally challenged [15]. It is well recognized that disruption of redox homeostasis alters gene expression and that the accumulation of oxidized proteins has a deleterious effect on cell function [16], [17]. Although the accumulation of carbonylated proteins is a general marker of oxidative stress in damaged and aging tissue, the monitoring of specific protein modifications can provide additional insight into the nature and site of oxidative stress. The peroxiredoxin family of antioxidant thiol proteins, which includes the mitochondrial protein peroxiredoxin 3 (Prx 3), is responsible for breaking down endogenous hydroperoxides [18]. As such excess hydrogen peroxide can hyperoxidize the active site cysteine of Prxs, thereby inactivating the protein [19], [20], [21], [22]. Although many studies have documented early life nutritional influences on reproductive function [5], [23]–[26], mechanisms underlying these associations are unclear. To date, no data exist regarding maternal nutritional effects on adult offspring ovarian oxidant status. fetched_contents.text: Pregnancy Under Pressure: Oxidative Stress as a Common Thread in Maternal Disorders Abstract Oxidative stress, defined as the imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidant defenses, plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of several pregnancy complications, notably preeclampsia (PE), gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), fetal growth restriction (FGR), and recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL). During normal pregnancy, low to moderate ROS levels support essential placental functions such as angiogenesis and trophoblast differentiation. However, excessive ROS production overwhelms antioxidant systems, leading to lipid peroxidation, protein and DNA damage, and impaired placental function. This review synthesizes current evidence linking oxidative stress to adverse pregnancy outcomes, highlighting key biomarkers such as malondialdehyde (MDA), 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), and 8-iso-prostaglandin F2α (8-iso-PGF2α). While antioxidant therapies—particularly vitamins C and E, selenium, and folic acid—have shown promise in reducing oxidative markers, their impact on clinical outcomes remains inconsistent. The variability in results underscores the need for standardized biomarker protocols and personalized treatment strategies based on genetic predispositions and baseline oxidative status. Future research may better harness antioxidant interventions to improve maternal–fetal health by addressing these gaps. Introduction Oxidative stress occurs when there is an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and the body’s antioxidant defense, resulting in cellular damage. ROS, such as superoxide anions, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals, are natural by-products of cellular metabolism. Under normal conditions, antioxidants neutralize ROS to maintain cellular stability. However, when ROS production surpasses the capacity of antioxidants, oxidative stress happens, causing damage to cellular lipids, proteins, and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) [1,2]. Figure 1 shows the balance between ROS and antioxidant defenses under normal conditions. When this balance is disturbed, oxidative stress happens, resulting in damage to cellular lipids, proteins, and DNA. During pregnancy, increased ROS production—especially in the placenta due to higher metabolic activity and oxygen changes—may lead to problems such as preeclampsia (PE), gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), fetal growth restriction (FGR), and recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL). During pregnancy, the impact of ROS on cellular components is especially signifi-cant due to the numerous physiological and metabolic changes that occur. These changes involve increased oxygen consumption, heightened mitochondrial activity, and increased blood flow to the placenta, all of which contribute to elevated ROS pro-duction. The placenta, a highly vascular and metabolically active organ, becomes a main site of ROS generation because of its high energy needs and varying oxygen levels. Evidence suggests that a low level of oxidative stress is not only unavoidable but may also be necessary for normal placental development. Specifically, moderate levels of ROS are involved in essential processes like trophoblast differentiation, blood vessel remodeling, and angiogenesis– the formation of new capillaries from existing blood vessels, crucial for tissue growth, including the placenta– via redox-sensitive signaling pathways. These controlled oxidative signals support proper implantation, spiral artery transformation, and placental blood vessel growth. However, if ROS production surpasses the antioxidant defense system’s capacity, the balance is lost, causing harmful oxidative stress that can impair placental function and lead to adverse pregnancy outcomes [3,4,5,6,7]. Nevertheless, excessive ROS production disrupts this balance, leading to damage in the following ways [6,8,9,10,11,12,13]: * ROS target polyunsaturated fatty acids in cellular membranes through lipid peroxidation, generating lipid radicals and end-products like malondialdehyde (MDA) that damage membrane integrity, increase cell permeability, and promote inflammation. In pregnancy, increased lipid peroxidation signifies oxidative stress, linked to conditions such as PE and FGR; * Proteins can be altered by ROS, affecting their structure and function. This can lead to a loss of enzyme activity, disrupted signaling, and impaired cellular processes. For instance, oxidative damage to antioxidant enzymes like superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase can reduce the cell’s ability to neutralize ROS, starting a self-perpetuating cycle of oxidative damage; * ROS can cause oxidative damage to DNA, leading to strand breaks, base modifications, and cross-linking, which can result in mutations and impaired cellular function. This DNA damage, caused by ROS, contributes to placental aging during pregnancy and has been linked to complications like RPL. Research demonstrates that adverse obstetric outcomes—including PE, GDM, FGR, and RPL—are frequently correlated with elevated biomarkers of oxidative stress such as MDA and 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), as well as reduced antioxidant capacity in maternal serum and placental tissues [14,15,16]. By elucidating the interactions between reactive oxygen species and various cellular constituents, we can deepen our understanding of oxidative stress mechanisms contributing to pregnancy pathologies, thereby informing biomarker discovery and therapeutic strategies [17,18,19]. 2. Women and providers often ask what a healthy diet for a pregnant woman should look like. The message should be “eat better, not more.” This can be achieved by basing diet on a variety of nutrient-dense, whole foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, healthy fats with omega-3 fatty acids that include nuts and seeds, and fish, in place of poorer quality highly processed foods. Such a diet embodies nutritional density and is less likely to be accompanied by excessive energy intake than the standard American diet consisting of increased intakes of processed foods, fatty red meat, and sweetened foods and beverages. Women who report “prudent” or “health-conscious” eating patterns before and/or during pregnancy may have fewer pregnancy complications and adverse child health outcomes. Comprehensive nutritional supplementation (multiple micronutrients plus balanced protein energy) among women with inadequate nutrition has been associated with improved birth outcomes, including decreased rates of low birthweight. A diet that severely restricts any macronutrient class should be avoided, specifically the ketogenic diet that lacks carbohydrates, the Paleo diet because of dairy restriction, and any diet characterized by excess saturated fats. User-friendly tools to facilitate a quick evaluation of dietary patterns with clear guidance on how to address dietary inadequacies and embedded support from trained healthcare providers are urgently needed. Recent evidence has shown that although excessive gestational weight gain predicts adverse perinatal outcomes among women with normal weight, the degree of prepregnancy obesity predicts adverse perinatal outcomes to a greater degree than gestational weight gain among women with obesity. Furthermore, low body mass index and insufficient gestational weight gain are associated with poor perinatal outcomes. Observational data have shown that first-trimester gain is the strongest predictor of adverse outcomes. Interventions beginning in early pregnancy or preconception are needed to prevent downstream complications for mothers and their children. For neonates, human milk provides personalized nutrition and is associated with short- and long-term health benefits for infants and mothers. Eating a healthy diet is a way for lactating mothers to support optimal health for themselves and their infants. Evidence on oxidative stress and related biomarkers in offspring indicates that maternal undernutrition is associated with measurable oxidative stress in placental and umbilical tissues, with downstream implications for offspring physiology. In pregnancy-focused evidence, oxidative stress is defined as an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidant defenses, and it can disrupt oxidative homeostasis, activate molecular pathways, and alter metabolic status [N3-F3]. The same source reports that placental tissue and umbilical fluid show upregulated markers such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), which are used to assess lipid peroxidation and DNA damage [N3-R1]. Another review emphasizes that maternal adherence to healthy dietary patterns during pregnancy may reduce DNA damage and lipid oxidation in mothers and offspring, supporting the idea that oxidative stress biomarkers can be influenced by nutrition [N3-R2]. In children, evidence of oxidative stress is also present: one study notes increased lipid peroxidation in small-for-growth (SGA) children, suggesting that oxidative stress markers can be detected in offspring tissues or fluids even outside the placenta [N3-R3]. A broader review on oxidative stress in pregnancy adds that oxidative stress can disrupt cell membrane oxidation, activate molecular pathways, and alter metabolic status, and that oxidative stress markers such as MDA and 8-OHdG are linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes [N3-R4].

Antioxidant defenses and inflammatory responses are also implicated. The pregnancy review explicitly states that excessive ROS production overwhelms antioxidant systems, leading to lipid peroxidation, protein and DNA damage, and impaired placental function [N3-F3]. It also notes that oxidative damage to antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase can reduce the cell’s ability to neutralize ROS, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of oxidative damage [N3-F3]. The same source points to inflammation as a consequence of oxidative stress: lipid radicals and end-products like MDA damage membrane integrity, increase cell permeability, and promote inflammation [N3-F3]. In addition, the oxidative stress review highlights that oxidative stress can disrupt cell membrane oxidation and activate a cascade of molecular pathways, implying that inflammation and signaling responses are not separate from the core oxidative stress mechanism [N3-R4].

The link between oxidative stress and ovarian dysfunction is suggested by the pregnancy review, which notes that oxidative stress can impair placental function and that oxidative stress conditions may underpin associations between early life nutritional adversity and altered later life physiological function [N3-F3]. While the evidence provided does not directly measure ovarian oxidative stress in offspring, it does establish that oxidative stress can compromise cellular function, impair antioxidant defenses, and alter metabolic status, making it a plausible mechanism by which maternal undernutrition may indirectly affect ovarian function [N3-F3]. The broader oxidative stress review also links oxidative stress to adverse pregnancy outcomes, which includes placental and fetal complications that can influence developmental programming and later reproductive health [N3-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports oxidative stress as a measurable biomarker in offspring, with markers such as MDA, 8-OHdG, and lipid peroxidation indicating damage and antioxidant depletion, while inflammation and enzyme dysfunction point to systemic oxidative stress responses [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-F3].

Mechanistic pathways connecting maternal undernutrition to ovarian function are best understood as a combination of placental transfer, nutrient restriction, fetal programming, epigenetic changes, endocrine signaling, and metabolic adaptation. First, maternal undernutrition is linked to fetal programming through intrauterine stress, with oxidative stress arising from conditions such as prenatal hypoxia, maternal under- and overnutrition, and excessive glucocorticoid exposure [N1-F1]. The same source explains that oxidative stress can act as a signaling factor in fetal programming via epigenetic mechanisms, linking oxidant molecules to dysregulation of specific target genes and potentially altering lifelong health and disease susceptibility [N1-F1]. This is consistent with a broader fetal programming perspective that maternal nutrition during pregnancy critically influences fetal development and shapes the offspring’s lifelong health and disease susceptibility [N1-R3].

The developmental windows most affected by maternal undernutrition are prenatal and postnatal periods, especially those involving placental and fetal redox regulation. The fetal programming review notes that the placenta becomes a main site of ROS generation due to its high metabolic activity and varying oxygen levels, and that placental redox state shifts during development from reduced to oxidized, acting as a driving force for cell differentiation [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that both nutrition and oxygenation are important for fetal growth, with reduced oxygenation independent of nutrition negatively impacting growth when nutrition is adequate [N1-F1]. This suggests that maternal undernutrition can affect fetal programming by altering placental transfer and nutrient availability, while also changing the fetal metabolic and redox environment. The review further states that maternal undernutrition leads to fetal adaptation by reducing metabolic energy supply to protect critical organs, which is described by the Thrifty Phenotype Hypothesis, and later expanded by the Predictive Adaptive Hypothesis to describe fetal responses to anticipated postnatal undernutrition [N1-F1].

Placental transfer and nutrient restriction are central mechanisms. The maternal nutrition review states that both maternal undernutrition and overnutrition reduce placental-fetal blood flows and stunt fetal growth, showing that placental transfer can be impaired by maternal nutrient status [N1-R2]. In the fetal programming context, placental transfer is tied to the redox environment and cell differentiation, with increased oxygen transfer during placentation initiating a switch in cellular redox state and driving fetal development [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that maternal undernutrition can restrict nutrient delivery, alter placental function, and disrupt fetal programming through oxidative stress and metabolic changes [N1-R2][N1-F1].

Epigenetic, endocrine, and metabolic pathways are also implicated. Epigenetic evidence indicates that maternal diet can influence the epigenome, with human studies showing that maternal periconceptional folic acid supplementation is linked to alterations in offspring DNA methylation [N5-R4]. The epigenetics literature also states that maternal diets or nutritional compositions contribute to the establishment of epigenetic profiles in the fetus that have a profound impact on individual development [N5-R3]. Evidence on undernutrition specifically notes that undernutrition can affect the epigenome by altering dietary methyl donors such as choline, betaine, folate, and other nutrients [N5-R5]. These epigenetic changes can persist into later life and may explain why maternal undernutrition can have long-term effects on offspring physiology [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Endocrine and metabolic pathways are implicated through oxidative stress and developmental programming. The pregnancy review explains that ROS serve as signaling molecules that induce transcription of genes important in oxygen sensing, cell differentiation, and proliferation [N1-F1]. It also states that oxidative stress can disrupt redox homeostasis, alter gene expression, and accumulate oxidized proteins, which have deleterious effects on cell function [N1-F1]. This mechanism connects maternal undernutrition to broader metabolic consequences, including altered gene regulation and impaired cellular function. The same source links oxidative stress to placental dysfunction and adverse pregnancy outcomes, reinforcing that maternal undernutrition can disrupt endocrine and metabolic signaling through redox imbalance [N1-F1].

In summary, the mechanistic pathways are: maternal undernutrition → altered placental transfer and nutrient restriction → oxidative stress and redox imbalance → fetal programming through epigenetic, endocrine, and metabolic changes → altered ovarian development and later reproductive function [N1-R2][N1-F1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence suggests that the most affected tissues and windows are the placenta and fetus during prenatal and postnatal development, with oxidative stress acting as a bridge between maternal nutrition and long-term physiological outcomes [N1-F1][N5-R5].

Contextual factors and limitations shaping the evidence base show that maternal undernutrition research spans pregnancy, lactation, and postnatal exposure, but the evidence base is uneven and subject to design and interpretation limits. First, the evidence base distinguishes pregnancy and lactation as different but related periods. The maternal nutrition review emphasizes that nutrition during pregnancy and lactation has lifelong consequences, with poor maternal nutritional status associated with abnormal fetal growth patterns and increased risks for offspring health [N4-F4]. Another review notes that maternal high-fat nutrition during pregnancy and lactation results in a maternal obese phenotype and affects maternal care during lactation, showing that lactation is not merely a postnatal endpoint but part of a continuum of maternal and offspring health [N4-R4]. This means that lactation-specific effects can differ from prenatal effects: pregnancy exposure primarily shapes fetal programming, while lactation exposure can influence maternal phenotype, maternal care, and postnatal offspring development [N4-F4][N4-R4].

A second contextual factor is the difference between pregnancy, lactation, and postnatal exposure in terms of developmental windows. The maternal nutrition review highlights that nutrition is critical during the reproductive period, including preconception through pregnancy and lactation, and that the continuum from preconception to pregnancy and lactation has received insufficient attention in the literature [N4-F4]. It also notes that offspring of mothers fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy and lactation enter puberty early and are hyperleptinaemic, illustrating how maternal nutrition during lactation can influence pubertal timing and metabolic outcomes [N4-R5]. This implies that lactation can shape offspring physiology in ways that are distinct from prenatal effects, particularly through hormonal and metabolic programming [N4-F4][N4-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a “first 1000 days” framework in which prenatal and postnatal nutrition interact, but the exact contribution of each period remains partially unresolved [N6-R3].

Study design limitations and confounding factors are substantial in human research. The maternal nutrition review states that most women in the United States do not meet nutrition and weight recommendations before and during pregnancy, and that observational data have shown that first-trimester gain is the strongest predictor of adverse outcomes [N4-F4]. It also notes that for many important questions, evidence is limited or uncertain, and that systematic reviews often assigned limited or no assignable evidence, underscoring the need for better-designed studies [N4-F4]. This limitation is important because human studies are often observational, confounded by socioeconomic, behavioral, and medical covariates, and unable to isolate the precise effects of maternal undernutrition from other determinants of offspring health [N4-F4]. The review further stresses that interventions beginning in early pregnancy or preconception are needed to prevent downstream complications, but the evidence base is still incomplete [N4-F4].

Lactation-specific effects may differ from prenatal effects because lactation is associated with maternal phenotype, maternal care, and postnatal metabolic programming. The maternal nutrition review explicitly states that maternal high-fat nutrition during pregnancy and lactation results in a maternal obese phenotype and affects maternal care during lactation [N4-R4]. The same source also reports that offspring of mothers fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy and lactation enter puberty early and are hyperleptinaemic [N4-R5]. These findings suggest that lactation can influence offspring pubertal timing and metabolic status through maternal metabolic changes and behavior, which may differ from prenatal effects that primarily shape fetal programming and long-term disease susceptibility [N4-R4][N4-R5]. However, the evidence provided does not establish that lactation-specific effects are qualitatively different in every case; rather, it shows that lactation can add a postnatal dimension to maternal and offspring health [N4-F4][N4-R4].

Overall, the evidence base is shaped by the distinction between pregnancy, lactation, and postnatal exposure, but human studies are limited by confounding, small evidence certainty, and the difficulty of isolating the effects of undernutrition from other factors [N4-F4][N4-R4]. The contextual picture is therefore one of overlapping but distinct windows of exposure, with lactation adding postnatal metabolic and behavioral influences that may differ from prenatal programming [N4-F4][N4-R4][N4-R5].

Evidence on offspring ovarian function after maternal undernutrition is strongest in animal studies, with some human and human-relevant findings indicating altered reproductive outcomes. The animal evidence is particularly direct: one study found that maternal undernutrition significantly reduced primordial and secondary follicle number in offspring, with reductions also observed in antral follicle number across all maternal undernutrition groups, and that these changes were associated with decreased mRNA levels of genes critical for follicle maturation and ovulation [N2-F2]. Another study reports that maternal low-protein diet programs low ovarian reserve in mice, and that evidence from animal models and women shows that maternal protein restriction during pregnancy and lactation impairs the development of the offspring ovarian system [N2-R2]. In addition, a cow study links transient maternal undernutrition with diminished ovarian reserve and potential suboptimal reproductive outcomes, while a sow experiment finds that maternal high-fat diet reduces the number of large and small follicles in offspring at pubertal stage [N2-R3][N2-R4]. These animal studies collectively support the conclusion that maternal undernutrition can reduce ovarian reserve and follicle development in offspring [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-F2].

Reproductive outcomes after maternal undernutrition include accelerated puberty, altered pubertal timing, and changes in ovarian function. The ovarian follicle study notes that maternal undernutrition advanced female pubertal onset in a manner dependent on the timing of undernutrition, and that the long-term consequence of accelerated puberty on ovarian function is unknown [N2-F2]. It also states that reproductive maturation and function are influenced by early life events, including nutrition, and that prenatal and postnatal nutritional environments interact to influence reproductive function in offspring [N2-F2]. A separate review on early-life nutrition and the female reproductive system brings together clinical observations in humans and indicates that early-life nutrition can affect the female reproductive system, though the provided excerpt does not give detailed offspring measures [N7-R1]. Human evidence is more suggestive than definitive: one review notes that nutrition and female fertility are interdependent, and that inadequate nutrition may interact with reproductive health in women [N7-R2]. Another human-relevant source reports that offspring of mothers fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy and lactation enter puberty early and are hyperleptinaemic, providing human-relevant evidence that maternal nutrition can alter pubertal timing and metabolic hormone profiles [N4-R5].

Hormonal profiles are also implicated. The ovarian follicle study notes that leptin acts as a metabolic signal to the central reproductive axis, with both stimulatory and inhibitory actions on ovulatory processes and ovarian steroidogenesis [N2-F2]. It also reports that leptin is a permissive neuro-regulatory factor for the onset of puberty [N2-F2]. This is relevant because maternal undernutrition can alter endocrine signaling and hormonal regulation, which may explain changes in puberty timing and reproductive function. The human-relevant evidence further connects maternal nutrition to hormonal and reproductive health, with one source stating that nutrition and female fertility are interdependent and that inadequate nutrition may interact with reproductive health in women [N7-R2]. However, the evidence provided does not give a detailed hormonal profile for maternal undernutrition offspring beyond these broader links [N7-R2].

Differences between animal models and human evidence are clear. ## Integrated final answer: How maternal undernutrition during pregnancy and lactation impacts ovarian function and oxidative stress in the offspring

Maternal undernutrition during pregnancy and lactation can have lasting effects on offspring ovarian function and oxidative stress. The evidence suggests a multi-level mechanism in which maternal nutrition alters placental transfer, nutrient restriction, fetal programming, and epigenetic regulation, while oxidative stress serves as a central mediator linking early-life adversity to later reproductive and metabolic consequences [N1-F1][N5-R3][N5-R5][N3-F3].

### 1. Mechanisms connecting maternal undernutrition to ovarian function

Maternal undernutrition primarily affects the fetal and neonatal developmental windows that are most sensitive to nutritional change. The placenta is a key tissue, because it is a highly vascular and metabolically active organ that becomes a main site of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation due to its high energy needs and varying oxygen levels [N1-F1]. During fetal development, placental redox state shifts from reduced to oxidized, acting as a driving force for cell differentiation and fetal growth [N1-F1]. Maternal undernutrition can therefore impair placental transfer and nutrient availability, reducing fetal growth and altering the fetal metabolic and redox environment [N1-R2][N1-F1].

This sets the stage for fetal programming. Maternal nutrition during pregnancy critically influences fetal development and shapes the offspring’s lifelong health and disease susceptibility [N1-R3]. Oxidative stress is also a central mechanism in fetal programming, arising from conditions such as prenatal hypoxia, maternal under- and overnutrition, and excessive glucocorticoid exposure [N1-F1]. The same source states that oxidant molecules can act as signaling factors in fetal programming via epigenetic mechanisms, linking oxidant molecules to dysregulation of specific target genes [N1-F1]. Epigenetic evidence further supports that maternal diet can influence the epigenome, with maternal periconceptional folic acid supplementation linked to alterations in offspring DNA methylation [N5-R4], and that maternal diets or nutritional compositions contribute to the establishment of epigenetic profiles in the fetus [N5-R3]. Undernutrition specifically can affect the epigenome by altering dietary methyl donors such as choline, betaine, folate, and other nutrients [N5-R5].

Endocrine and metabolic pathways are also implicated. ROS serve as signaling molecules that induce transcription of genes important in oxygen sensing, cell differentiation, and proliferation [N1-F1]. Oxidative stress can disrupt redox homeostasis, alter gene expression, and accumulate oxidized proteins, which have deleterious effects on cell function [N1-F1]. This means maternal undernutrition can influence ovarian development through both direct metabolic and indirect epigenetic-endocrine pathways [N1-F1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

### 2. Evidence on offspring ovarian function after maternal undernutrition

The strongest evidence for offspring ovarian dysfunction comes from animal studies. One study found that maternal undernutrition significantly reduced primordial and secondary follicle number in offspring, with reductions also observed in antral follicle number across all maternal undernutrition groups, and that these changes were associated with decreased mRNA levels of genes critical for follicle maturation and ovulation [N2-F2]. Another study reports that maternal low-protein diet programs low ovarian reserve in mice, and that evidence from animal models and women shows that maternal protein restriction during pregnancy and lactation impairs the development of the offspring ovarian system [N2-R2]. A cow study links transient maternal undernutrition with diminished ovarian reserve and potential suboptimal reproductive outcomes, while a sow experiment finds that maternal high-fat diet reduces the number of large and small follicles in offspring at the pubertal stage [N2-R3][N2-R4]. These findings collectively support the conclusion that maternal undernutrition is associated with reduced ovarian reserve and follicle development in offspring [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-F2].

Reproductive outcomes after maternal undernutrition include accelerated puberty and altered pubertal timing. The ovarian follicle study notes that maternal undernutrition advanced female pubertal onset in a manner dependent on the timing of undernutrition, and that the long-term consequence of this accelerated puberty on ovarian function is unknown [N2-F2]. It also states that reproductive maturation and function are influenced by early life events, including nutrition, and that prenatal and postnatal nutritional environments interact to influence reproductive function in offspring [N2-F2]. Human-relevant evidence further supports this pattern: one review notes that nutrition and female fertility are interdependent, and that inadequate nutrition may interact with reproductive health in women [N7-R2]. Another human-relevant source reports that offspring of mothers fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy and lactation enter puberty early and are hyperleptinaemic, providing evidence that maternal nutrition can alter pubertal timing and metabolic hormone profiles [N4-R5].

Hormonal profiles are also implicated. The ovarian follicle study notes that leptin acts as a metabolic signal to the central reproductive axis, with both stimulatory and inhibitory actions on ovulatory processes and ovarian steroidogenesis [N2-F2]. It also reports that leptin is a permissive neuro-regulatory factor for the onset of puberty [N2-F2]. This is relevant because maternal undernutrition can alter endocrine signaling and hormonal regulation, which may explain changes in puberty timing and reproductive function [N2-F2][N7-R2].

### 3. Evidence on oxidative stress and related biomarkers in offspring

Evidence on oxidative stress in offspring indicates that maternal undernutrition is associated with measurable oxidative stress in placental and umbilical tissues. Oxidative stress is defined as an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidant defenses, and it can disrupt oxidative homeostasis, activate molecular pathways, and alter metabolic status [N3-F3]. The placental and umbilical evidence shows upregulated markers such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), which are used to assess lipid peroxidation and DNA damage [N3-R1]. Another review emphasizes that maternal adherence to healthy dietary patterns during pregnancy may reduce DNA damage and lipid oxidation in mothers and offspring, supporting the idea that oxidative stress biomarkers can be influenced by nutrition [N3-R2]. In children, evidence of oxidative stress is also present: one study notes increased lipid peroxidation in small-for-growth (SGA) children, suggesting that oxidative stress markers can be detected in offspring tissues or fluids even outside the placenta [N3-R3].

Antioxidant defenses and inflammatory responses are also implicated. Excessive ROS production overwhelms antioxidant systems, leading to lipid peroxidation, protein and DNA damage, and impaired placental function [N3-F3]. Oxidative damage to antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase can reduce the cell’s ability to neutralize ROS, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of oxidative damage [N3-F3]. The same source points to inflammation as a consequence of oxidative stress: lipid radicals and end-products like MDA damage membrane integrity, increase cell permeability, and promote inflammation [N3-F3]. A broader review on oxidative stress in pregnancy adds that oxidative stress can disrupt cell membrane oxidation and activate a cascade of molecular pathways, implying that inflammation and signaling responses are not separate from the core oxidative stress mechanism [N3-R4].

The link between oxidative stress and ovarian dysfunction is suggested by the pregnancy review, which notes that oxidative stress can impair placental function and that oxidative stress conditions may underpin associations between early life nutritional adversity and altered later life physiological function [N3-F3]. While the evidence provided does not directly measure ovarian oxidative stress in offspring, it does establish that oxidative stress can compromise cellular function, impair antioxidant defenses, and alter metabolic status, making it a plausible mechanism by which maternal undernutrition may indirectly affect ovarian function [N3-F3]. The broader oxidative stress review also links oxidative stress to adverse pregnancy outcomes, which includes placental and fetal complications that can influence developmental programming and later reproductive health [N3-R4].

### 4. Contextual factors and limitations shaping the evidence base

The evidence base spans pregnancy, lactation, and postnatal exposure, but the evidence is uneven and subject to design and interpretation limitations. The maternal nutrition review emphasizes that nutrition during pregnancy and lactation has lifelong consequences, with poor maternal nutritional status associated with abnormal fetal growth patterns and increased risks for offspring health [N4-F4]. Another review notes that maternal high-fat nutrition during pregnancy and lactation results in a maternal obese phenotype and affects maternal care during lactation, showing that lactation is not merely a postnatal endpoint but part of a continuum of maternal and offspring health [N4-R4]. This means lactation-specific effects can differ from prenatal effects: pregnancy exposure primarily shapes fetal programming, while lactation exposure can influence maternal phenotype, maternal care, and postnatal offspring development [N4-F4][N4-R4].

A second contextual factor is the difference between pregnancy, lactation, and postnatal exposure in terms of developmental windows. The maternal nutrition review highlights that nutrition is critical during the reproductive period, including preconception through pregnancy and lactation, and that the continuum from preconception to pregnancy and lactation has received insufficient attention in the literature [N4-F4]. It also notes that offspring of mothers fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy and lactation enter puberty early and are hyperleptinaemic, illustrating how maternal nutrition during lactation can influence pubertal timing and metabolic outcomes [N4-R5]. This implies that lactation can shape offspring physiology in ways that are distinct from prenatal effects, particularly through hormonal and metabolic programming [N4-F4][N4-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a “first 1000 days” framework in which prenatal and postnatal nutrition interact, but the exact contribution of each period remains partially unresolved [N6-R3].

Study design limitations and confounding factors are substantial in human research. The maternal nutrition review states that most women in the United States do not meet nutrition and weight recommendations before and during pregnancy, and that observational data have shown that first-trimester gain is the strongest predictor of adverse outcomes [N4-F4]. It also notes that for many important questions, evidence is limited or uncertain, and that systematic reviews often assigned limited or no assignable evidence, underscoring the need for better-designed studies [N4-F4]. This limitation is important because human studies are often observational, confounded by socioeconomic, behavioral, and medical covariates, and unable to isolate the precise effects of maternal undernutrition from other determinants of offspring health [N4-F4]. The review further stresses that interventions beginning in early pregnancy or preconception are needed to prevent downstream complications, but the evidence base is still incomplete [N4-F4].

Lactation-specific effects may differ from prenatal effects because lactation is associated with maternal phenotype, maternal care, and postnatal metabolic programming. The maternal nutrition review explicitly states that maternal high-fat nutrition during pregnancy and lactation results in a maternal obese phenotype and affects maternal care during lactation [N4-R4]. The same source also reports that offspring of mothers fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy and lactation enter puberty early and are hyperleptinaemic [N4-R5]. These findings suggest that lactation can influence offspring pubertal timing and metabolic status through maternal metabolic changes and behavior, which may differ from prenatal effects that primarily shape fetal programming and long-term disease susceptibility [N4-R4][N4-R5]. However, the evidence provided does not establish that lactation-specific effects are qualitatively different in every case; rather, it shows that lactation can add a postnatal dimension to maternal and offspring health [N4-F4][N4-R4].

### 5. Differences between animal models and human evidence

Animal studies are stronger for direct measures of ovarian function. They can directly measure follicle numbers, follicle stages, and gene expression, making them strong sources for mechanistic understanding [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R3]. In contrast, human evidence is more suggestive and less standardized. The maternal nutrition review notes that most women in the United States do not meet nutrition and weight recommendations before and during pregnancy, and that evidence for many important questions is limited or uncertain [N4-F4]. The review also highlights that systematic reviews often assigned limited or no assignable evidence, underscoring the need for better-designed studies [N4-F4]. This means human evidence is suggestive but not yet robust enough to establish the same level of detail as animal findings [N4-F4]. The human-relevant evidence provided also points to the importance of nutrition in pregnancy and lactation for lifelong consequences, but it does not offer the same direct measures of ovarian reserve as animal studies [N4-F4][N7-R1][N7-R2].

### 6. Bottom line

Overall, the evidence suggests that maternal undernutrition during pregnancy and lactation can impact offspring ovarian function and oxidative stress through a combination of placental transfer, nutrient restriction, fetal programming, epigenetic changes, and oxidative stress. Animal studies show reduced ovarian reserve and follicle development, while human evidence supports the broader idea that maternal nutrition can influence reproductive health and pubertal outcomes [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-F2][N4-R5][N7-R2]. Oxidative stress appears to be a central mediator, with markers such as MDA, 8-OHdG, and lipid peroxidation indicating damage and antioxidant depletion, and with antioxidant defenses and inflammation also implicated [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-F3]. However, human research is limited by confounding, small evidence certainty, and the difficulty of isolating maternal undernutrition from other factors [N4-F4]. The contextual picture is therefore one of overlapping but distinct windows of exposure, with lactation adding postnatal metabolic and behavioral influences that may differ from prenatal programming [N4-F4][N4-R4][N4-R5].
